licence.tune: public domain: printed in the United States in 1926 (before 1931); the page calls it "Traditional". Known as Sulzer's Shema, but it is not the Shema Salomon Sulzer (died 1890) printed in Schir Zion (vol. 1, No. 104 in Joseph Sulzer's revised edition), which shares only its meter, its first note and its closing "Adoshem echad". Geoffrey Goldberg (Journal of Synagogue Music, 2019) argues it should be attributed to the cantor Jacob Beimel (died 1944), whose manuscript shows it taking shape, and calls this 1926 page its first printed occurrence. The 1926 book, compiled by Israel Goldfarb (died 1967) and Samuel E. Goldfarb (died 1978), is melody only throughout, one line for cantor or congregation with no harmony, and marks its own work by name ("I. Goldfarb" on No. 8, "Adapted by I. Goldfarb" on No. 26); this Shema it marks "Traditional", so nothing of theirs is in what we sing, and they are credited as its earliest known printing, not as makers.
